- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and forecast spikes upward, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- If sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast is rising, cap the forecast at 1–2% below the 14-day moving average to prevent overreaction.  
- If the last 3–5 days show strong mean reversion (price drops after a spike), adjust forecast to slightly underperform the prior 10-day average.  
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.3–0.7), reduce forecast volatility by smoothing 3–5 day moving average of forecast vs true.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcome is consistently below forecast, apply a 3–5% downward bias to future predictions unless sentiment is strongly bullish.  
- If sentiment is consistently 1.0 (strong bullish) and forecast is rising, check for overfitting — if price has been rising for 5+ days, reduce forecast slope by 10–15%.  
- If sentiment is 0.0–0.2 (bearish) and forecast is rising, treat as “false breakout” — reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.  
- For 30d forecasts, if true outcome is consistently 2–3% below forecast, apply a 2–3% downward correction for next period unless sentiment is strong bullish.  
- If sentiment is high and price is trending upward, forecast should not exceed 1.5x the 14-day average unless sentiment is >0.85.  
- If sentiment is low and forecast is high, apply a “mean reversion” correction: forecast = prior 10-day average + 0.5x (true - prior 10-day avg).
